lessons.title: When you stop drafting from scratch
lessons.subtitle: From a blank document to a Claude brief
lessons.voiceAnchor: You already have tools. The relevant question is how to combine them.

props.title: Write a better brief for Claude
props.scenario: A customer emails you asking for a solution by Friday. The prompt below is incomplete. Add a role, the relevant context, a clear task and a specific output format.
props.startingPrompt: Draft a reply to the customer.

criteria.label: Names a role, such as sales assistant, master craftsperson or HR partner
Provides context about the customer and subject
States the task explicitly: confirm, ask for details or escalate
Defines the format, including word limit and tone
Includes at least one open question for the customer

sections.title: Two drafts, one stopwatch
sections.content:
Customer Alpha, fictional, writes about a late delivery. You answer twice: once by hand, once with Claude drafting for you.

Start the stopwatch. For both versions, record drafting time, factual errors, corrections needed and tone. The Claude version stays an internal draft until a person approves it.

No promise of a fixed time saving, no promise of equal quality. Your comparison decides whether this workflow is worth anything here.
sections.keyTakeaway: The blank document is one starting point of two. The brief is the one you can measure.

sections.title: When the blank document is the wrong starting point
sections.content:
A blank document hands you every decision and every sentence to write. A Claude draft moves the starting point from writing to briefing and review.

So why do so many still start at zero? Three reasons, none of them stupid:
- Habit: routines drilled in over years
- Control: you know exactly what went into the text
- Professional identity: for a controller, writing is part of the job

One question per task: does the brief cut effort without weakening accuracy or tone?
sections.keyTakeaway: Measured quality and working time decide the starting point. Not habit.

sections.title: The three-part Claude brief
sections.content:
Open Claude. Do not type "Write a reply to this customer inquiry." That hands the model every decision that belongs to you.

Three constraints instead of a request:

**Role:** "You are my sales assistant at an 80-person mechanical-engineering company in Bavaria. Use a pragmatic, direct and plain-spoken tone."

**Context:** paste the customer email, provided its contents are approved for the tool.

**Task:** "Draft a reply. Confirm Friday as the target, but ask the customer for the batch number and number of affected parts. Keep the tone polite and current. Use fewer than 150 words."

Then you read it. Fix every wrong statement, every uncovered commitment and every tonal slip before it goes out. Measure time and correction effort instead of assuming the Claude draft is better.
sections.keyTakeaway: Role, context and task narrow the draft. An open request does not.

sections.title: Why three constraints are enough
sections.content:
Each constraint takes one degree of freedom away from the model.

**Role:** sets perspective and style. In this example the draft sounds like an industrial company, not like startup advertising.

**Context:** supplies what the draft needs to know. Only data approved for the selected tool.

**Task:** makes the result checkable. Fewer than 150 words, one confirmation, one question, a defined tone.

Drop one constraint and the text turns generic, or the model invents its own assumptions. That is a briefing error. It says nothing about the model.

Your work shifts. Not formulating every sentence, but setting the task, checking the facts and approving the text.
sections.keyTakeaway: The model writes the draft. Facts, reasoning and approval stay with you.

quiz.questionText: Which three elements make an effective prompt?

answerOptions.text: Politeness, length and closing phrase
Role, context and task
Question, example and instruction
Introduction, main section and conclusion

quiz.explanation: Role, context and task. RCTFC adds format and constraints later.

quiz.questionText: Where does your time belong in an AI-assisted role?

answerOptions.text: Spend most of the time typing and little time reviewing
Define the task, brief the model and check quality instead of doing all the typing
Give Claude more time and review less yourself
Delegate every task to Claude without review

quiz.explanation: Hand over the drafting when the task suits it. Judgment and approval stay with you.

lessons.title: Why I use my IDE differently now
lessons.subtitle: Orchestrate instead of executing every step
lessons.voiceAnchor: In some engineering teams, developers now spend less time typing code and more time specifying and reviewing it.

props.title: RCTFC: your first structured brief
props.scenario: You are a sales manager and want Claude to draft a quotation summary. Complete all five RCTFC fields.

role.hint: Who should perform the task? For example, a sales assistant in mechanical engineering.

context.hint: Provide enough background about the company, industry and customer relationship to establish the situation.

task.hint: What exactly should be produced: a quotation, summary or follow-up question?

format.hint: Define the structure, length and output format, such as Markdown, no more than 200 words and three sections.

constraints.hint: State exclusions, such as promotional language or unapproved prices.

sections.title: From my own working week, anonymized
sections.content:
I work as a data engineer at a large US technology company. The experienced developers around me increasingly generate a first code version from a specification. What they do not hand over: inspecting the repository, reading the output, running tests, correcting defects, approving the change.

The IDE stays open for navigation, debugging and review. The shift is smaller than the hype claims. Less time typing routine code, more time on what gets built and whether it holds.

The same division of work travels outside software engineering. The task needs a describable output and a review step that holds.
sections.keyTakeaway: Typing is only one part of the work. Judgment determines whether the result is usable.

sections.title: Orchestrating instead of executing
sections.content:
Executing means every production step is yours. Typing, formatting, calculating, carrying data from tool to tool.

Orchestrating means you **describe the result you need**, give the system the permitted inputs and check what comes back. You correct the errors. The final action is yours.

Claude produces output from instructions and context. Nothing more. It understands no intent, verifies no fact on its own, carries no responsibility. So you fix the brief, the permitted data and the review criteria up front.

Hand over bounded, reviewable production steps. Decisions, accountability and sensitive actions stay with a person.
sections.keyTakeaway: You specify and check. The routine goes to the system.

sections.title: What changes in your role
sections.content:
The developer is only the nearest example. The same shift is waiting in other departments:

- **Sales:** Claude drafts the quotation. Pricing strategy and every commitment stay with you.
- **Finance:** Claude drafts a read-only SQL query. You validate it and read the figures.
- **HR:** Claude drafts the job advertisement. You check the legal, factual and organizational requirements.
- **Operations:** Claude structures the process data. You decide what changes.

The skill that counts was never typing. Applying domain knowledge, spotting the missing information, judging whether the result fits. That is the work.

AI assistance can cut routine production. It does not cut professional responsibility or the need for expertise.
sections.keyTakeaway: AI for the bounded production work. Domain judgment and accountability stay with the role owner.

quiz.questionText: Which part of an AI-assisted role can often be reduced?

answerOptions.text: Your ability to make decisions
Routine typing and first-draft production
Customer relationships
Domain expertise

quiz.explanation: Routine drafting can shrink. Judgment, domain expertise and customer relationships stay, and often take a larger share of the work.

quiz.questionText: What distinguishes model output from an accountable work result?

answerOptions.text: The model owns final approval
Model output requires defined review; people and organizations retain accountability and approval
The model automatically checks every statement against all relevant sources
The model may make binding commitments without approval

quiz.explanation: Model output comes from inputs and configuration. It becomes a work result only through task-specific review, documented approval and someone who carries the responsibility.

lessons.title: Claude in the workflow: you specify and review
lessons.subtitle: Three basic patterns for AI orchestration
lessons.voiceAnchor: Your work is to specify the result, provide the relevant context and judge the output.

props.title: Which prompt provides the clearest direction?
props.scenario: Three colleagues want Claude to draft a quotation for the same customer and starting situation. Which prompt provides enough information for a useful first draft?

candidates.label: Option A: vague request
candidates.prompt: Draft a quotation for the customer who called today.
candidates.critique: No role, usable context or output requirements are supplied. Claude would have to infer the company, industry, tone, product and commercial terms.

candidates.label: Option B: partly specified
candidates.prompt: As a sales assistant in mechanical engineering, draft a quotation for the explicitly fictional Customer Alpha for three fictional XR-200 sample machines. Delivery in December.
candidates.critique: Role, context and task are present. The prompt still lacks a format and constraints for length, sections, tone, price and payment terms.

candidates.label: Option C: structured brief
candidates.prompt: Role: sales assistant in mechanical engineering. Context: explicitly fictional Customer Alpha has 12 employees and needs three fictional XR-200 sample machines. Use a pragmatic tone and informal address. Task: prepare an internal quotation draft with three line items. Use placeholders for delivery date, payment term and price, and mark each for review. Format: Markdown, no more than 280 words. Constraints: do not invent commitments or use promotional language.
candidates.critique: This RCTFC brief defines the role, context, task, format and constraints. It should produce a reviewable draft without inventing commercial terms.

sections.title: Three basic patterns
sections.content:
**Pattern 1: Drafting**

You need a first version: email, report, presentation. Claude delivers V1, you turn it into V2.

> "Draft V1 of [output] using [approved context]. Follow [tone]. Length: [limit]."

Note time and correction effort. Every time.

**Pattern 2: Analysis**

You have data or text and want something specific pulled out or summarized.

> "Here is [input]. Extract [fields]. Summarize [patterns]. Format: [table, list or prose]. State uncertainty."

The workflow depends on size, sensitivity and how much checking the output needs.

**Pattern 3: Research**

You need evidence. Take a tool that can search, then open the cited primary sources.

> "Research [topic]. Answer [specific questions]. Use [required source types]. Return [structure] with links and publication dates."

Three patterns cover a large share of knowledge work. The task-specific check is still yours.
sections.keyTakeaway: Drafting, analysis and research require different inputs and review criteria.

sections.title: Write the context once
sections.content:
Typing the same company context every week wastes time. A Claude Project holds stable, non-confidential context and the communication rules for recurring tasks.

Create a Project called "Sales drafts" and use an instruction such as:

```
I work in sales at an 80-person mechanical-engineering company
in Bavaria with customers in Germany and Austria.
Our products are specialist machines for metal processing.
Typical price range: EUR 15,000 to EUR 200,000 per machine.

Customer communication rules:
- Informal address for established customers; formal address for new customers
- Pragmatic, plain language
- No buzzwords or promotional claims
- Do not make delivery, price or contract commitments without approval
```

Only what is approved for permanent Project context goes in. A later request carries the case, not the rules:

> "New-customer inquiry for three Type X machines. Draft a reply and mark missing commercial details."
sections.keyTakeaway: Approved recurring context once, in the Project. Sensitive and case-specific material stays out.

sections.title: Narrow, medium, deep
sections.content:
V1 rarely lands. When you revise, say how much should change and why.

**Narrow:** change one sentence. "Remove the second paragraph. Make the tone one level more direct."

**Medium:** change the structure. "Reorder the arguments and put the strongest evidence first."

**Deep:** new premise, new attempt. "V1 is too generic. Rewrite it with a direct tone and focus on the customer's time cost rather than our features."

The model does the rewrite. Whether the result holds up professionally is still your call.
sections.keyTakeaway: Narrow, medium or deep: the level follows the defect, not your mood.

quiz.questionText: Which three basic patterns support AI orchestration?

answerOptions.text: Automating, delegating and reviewing
Drafting, analysis and research
Writing, reading and translating
Creating, checking and distributing

quiz.explanation: Drafting creates an initial text, analysis structures supplied input and research gathers evidence from sources.

quiz.questionText: Why use a reusable Claude Project brief instead of repeating the same context?

answerOptions.text: It keeps approved recurring context available within the Project
Claude can process only one instruction per session
Every piece of context must be documented permanently
Projects always store more text than regular chats

quiz.explanation: A Project brief avoids repeating stable, approved context. Review it whenever the role, policy or data boundary changes.

lessons.title: Ten tasks to test for AI assistance
lessons.subtitle: Concrete use cases and prompts
lessons.voiceAnchor: Ten bounded examples show where drafting or analysis may reduce routine work.

props.title: Which task should you delegate in your role?
props.scenario: Select your role. For each of three situations from a mid-sized company, distinguish a bounded AI-assisted workflow from manual work or unsafe automation.

roles.label: Sales / Account Management
roles.description: Field sales, inside sales and sales management

scenarios.question: A prospective customer sends five technical questions at 16:40. A response is due today, and your workday ends at 17:00.

options.label: Write every response manually and work until 18:30.
options.explanation: Working by hand is legitimate for sensitive questions. It never tests whether a structured draft takes the routine off you.

options.label: Wait until tomorrow because careful work takes time.
options.explanation: Waiting is right when facts are missing. Once the answers exist, a reviewed draft still makes today's deadline.

options.label: Brief Claude with the role, approved email context, five required answers and a 200-word limit. Review every technical claim and send only after approval.
options.explanation: First draft, technical check and approval stay separate. That is how it should run.

options.label: Find and adapt an old template.
options.explanation: A template helps. It does not replace the case-specific edit, and it carries old wording along.

scenarios.question: At 15:00 you have a practice meeting with fictional Customer Alpha. Three sample emails and the latest notes are four weeks old.

options.label: Open the CRM five minutes before the meeting and rely on memory.
options.explanation: A quick look misses the open points. Define your preparation questions and read the source material properly.

options.label: Ask Claude to extract open points, documented concerns and three questions from the approved sample emails and notes. Review the result before the meeting.
options.explanation: This is the analysis pattern from Lesson 3: structured extraction from a bounded source set.

options.label: Ask a colleague who knows the fictional case.
options.explanation: A colleague who knows the case adds context. Recollection is no substitute for opening the records.

options.label: Cancel the meeting because there is too little preparation time.
options.explanation: Three emails and a few notes are not worth a cancellation. Small source set, checkable preparation.

scenarios.question: For the weekly review, you need the top 20 customers by revenue from a database, but you do not write SQL.

options.label: Ask Controlling and wait two days.
options.explanation: Controlling still reviews the numbers. A validated read-only query shortens the first step.

options.label: Rebuild the analysis in Excel by hand.
options.explanation: It works, and it is fragile. Manual joins, repeated every week, add avoidable error risk.

options.label: Provide Claude with the table schema and ask for read-only SQL. Have a qualified person review it before running it.
options.explanation: Claude drafts the query. That grants no database access, and the result is still unchecked.

options.label: Skip the analysis.
options.explanation: Leaving out the evidence weakens sales planning. No upside anywhere.

roles.label: HR / People / Management
roles.description: Recruiting, staff communication and personnel decisions

scenarios.question: You need a job advertisement today for a 20-hour-per-week mechanical-engineering working-student position.

options.label: Copy a 2023 advertisement and change the date.
options.explanation: The old advertisement carries outdated facts and language. It needs a full review either way.

options.label: Create an HR Project with approved company context and tone. Ask for a draft for the working-student role and verify every condition.
options.explanation: Maintained context shortens the brief. Legal, factual and contractual terms still go past a person.

options.label: Hire an agency and wait three weeks.
options.explanation: An agency has its place. You do not need one for a first draft.

options.label: Ask ChatGPT to write a generic advertisement without company or role context.
options.explanation: Without role, company and tone you get stock text, and the model invents requirements.

scenarios.question: You need an internal email about a new remote-work rule: two days per week from June for 80 employees, written without HR jargon.

options.label: Spend three hours polishing the wording before management review.
options.explanation: The policy decision needs care. The wording does not. Separate the two.

options.label: Brief Claude with the HR role, approved policy facts, reasons, 180-word limit, plain tone and an FAQ link. Review with the responsible people before sending.
options.explanation: A structured draft saves the writing. Decision, sign-off and accountability stay where they were.

options.label: Ask an executive assistant to draft it.
options.explanation: That is a legitimate allocation decision. It also hands routine drafting to another person.

options.label: Announce the rule only in the monthly meeting.
options.explanation: Nobody can look up a spoken announcement. The rule needs a text everyone can reach.

scenarios.question: A manager asks: "What did we decide about remote work in January?"

options.label: Say you do not remember and search your email later.
options.explanation: The answer is in the decision record, not in your memory.

options.label: Search Notion, file storage, email and the CRM manually for 20 minutes.
options.explanation: Sometimes a manual search is all you have. Four separate stores make it slow and leave gaps.

options.label: Query an approved decision log through Claude or an Obsidian assistant: "Remote-work decision, January 2026. Cite the source note."
options.explanation: AI-assisted retrieval holds only when it names the authoritative record and you open it.

options.label: Say you will check and then fail to follow up.
options.explanation: Promised and forgotten. Exactly what a decision log exists to prevent.

roles.label: Operations / Production / IT
roles.description: Process control, production management and IT coordination

scenarios.question: A fictional ERP export has 4,800 rows with inconsistent labels for Customer Alpha and mixed date formats.

options.label: Write an Excel macro and spend four hours debugging it.
options.explanation: A macro pays off for a recurring, controlled process. Test the normalization rules first, or you debug into the void.

options.label: Give Claude a fictional CSV and explicit normalization rules. Request a change log and validate the result before replacing any source data.
options.explanation: Bounded transformation, reversible output, a fixed review point. That is a good test case.

options.label: Assign an intern for two days.
options.explanation: Manual cleanup is slow, and the next export starts the same game. Not reproducible either.

options.label: Leave the data unchanged because the dashboard can tolerate it.
options.explanation: Three spellings, three rows in the dashboard. Every total is wrong.

scenarios.question: A 45-minute production-management meeting transcript is available. Action items must be discussed in tomorrow's stand-up.

options.label: Read the complete transcript and extract every item manually.
options.explanation: You have to read it anyway. A structured extraction can prepare the first pass.

options.label: Ask Claude to extract decisions, action items with owners and dates, and open questions into a table. Verify each item against the transcript.
options.explanation: Structured extraction, and the transcript stays the authoritative source.

options.label: Ask each participant to submit their own action items.
options.explanation: Asking participants helps. Everyone sends a different format, and the cross-team decision is missing.

options.label: Remember the three most important items and ignore the rest.
options.explanation: Unrecorded actions come back later. As an escalation.

scenarios.question: Management needs a weekly status across five projects: highlights, problems and next week.

options.label: Reserve 90 minutes every Friday to write it from scratch.
options.explanation: It works. A weekly report with a fixed structure is asking for a reviewed template.

options.label: Provide an approved activity list and ask Claude for a factual three-section draft: highlights, problems and next week. Remove unsupported claims before sending.
options.explanation: Drafting with a stable structure. Then you time it instead of assuming a saving.

options.label: Hold a status call with every project lead and then summarize it.
options.explanation: Decisions need conversations. Routine updates you collect asynchronously and check afterwards.

options.label: Tell management there will be no report this week.
options.explanation: Skipping an agreed report hides the project risks. And costs you credibility.

sections.title: Tasks 1 to 5
sections.content:
**Task 1: Draft emails from bullet points**
> "Fictional notes: Customer Alpha, delayed delivery, unverified target date, request for batch number. Create an internal email draft and mark every commitment for review."

**Task 2: Prepare for meetings from approved records**
> "I have a practice meeting with Customer Alpha at 15:00. Here are fictional sample emails and notes. List open points, documented interests and three questions. Do not infer motives."

**Task 3: Extract action items from a meeting**
> "Here is an approved or fictional transcript. Extract decisions, action items with owners and dates, and open questions. Mark uncertainty."

**Task 4: Research for a decision**
> "Compare accounting systems using current official sources. Separate documented features, current prices and unresolved contract or privacy questions."

**Task 5: Draft a form**
> "Fictional Customer Alpha needs a fictional sample machine. Fill the quotation template only with confirmed information; keep price, payment term and delivery date as reviewed placeholders."
sections.keyTakeaway: Email drafts, meeting prep, action items, research, form drafts: five candidates for bounded assistance.

sections.title: Tasks 6 to 10
sections.content:
**Task 6: Clean data in Excel**
> "Here is a fictional CSV export with inconsistent labels for Customer Alpha and mixed date formats. Normalize it according to the supplied rules and log every change."

**Task 7: Structure a presentation from source material**
> "Here are approved notes and three charts. Propose a structure with source references and mark unsupported statements."

**Task 8: Draft SQL for a database lookup**
> "In a test database, I need revenue by fictional customer for the last quarter. Write read-only SQL and explain every assumption."

**Task 9: Translate and localize**
> "Here is a fictional German customer letter. Translate it into English and flag legally or culturally uncertain wording for review."

**Task 10: Draft a status update**
> "Here is an approved activity list. Prepare a factual draft with highlights, problems, uncertainties and next steps."
sections.keyTakeaway: No AI specialist needed for any of this. Data control and review still are.

sections.title: The main source of friction
sections.content:
Ten ordinary knowledge tasks. Testing one needs no AI program and no large project. It can need your organization's approval before any data moves.

Take one task with low-risk or fictional data. Fix the input, the expected result and the review criteria. Then run it both ways, by hand and with Claude, and compare time, accuracy and correction effort.

Scale only when the test shows a benefit and the data use is approved. Not before.
sections.keyTakeaway: One bounded task, one measured result. Expand after that.

quiz.questionText: What commonly prevents practical AI adoption in a mid-sized company?

answerOptions.text: The technical complexity of every tool
Treating every low-risk experiment as a large program instead of defining a bounded test
A lack of any time for training
The purchase price of all AI tools

quiz.explanation: The apparatus around the test becomes the obstacle. A low-risk, reversible use case needs defined inputs, review criteria and approval. Nothing else.

quiz.questionText: How should you estimate the effort required to start one use case?

answerOptions.text: Measure preparation, execution and review time for the actual task
Thirty minutes in every case
Three hours in every case
Assume three minutes without measuring the workflow

quiz.explanation: There is no universal three-minute estimate. Record setup, execution and review time for the selected use case.

lessons.title: AI-Native Fluency self-assessment
lessons.subtitle: Ten scenarios across five dimensions
lessons.voiceAnchor: Use the same criteria now and later so the comparison is meaningful.

sections.title: The five dimensions
sections.content:
This test does not score ability. It scores behavior. Five dimensions, a diagnostic model, not an externally validated competency standard.

**1. Drafting:** do first drafts come out of Claude, or do you write every version yourself?

**2. Delegation:** do you hand over whole, bounded tasks with context, or single fragments?

**3. Automation:** do approved workflows run on their own, or does every step wait for your click?

**4. Knowledge:** can you query an approved knowledge base and cite every record, or does it sit in heads and inboxes?

**5. Governance:** can you classify data and apply your organization's rules, GDPR and the EU AI Act included?

Each dimension has five levels:
- Level 0: never
- Level 1: occasional, unstructured
- Level 2: regular and deliberate
- Level 3: default for suitable tasks
- Level 4: consistent, with defined controls

Score what you do. Not what you intend.
sections.keyTakeaway: Record the starting point now, run the same assessment later.

sections.title: The test: ten scenarios
sections.content:
Read each scenario and pick what you **actually do today**. Not what you plan to.

**Scenario 1, Drafting:** A customer email requires a reply today.
A) I open Google Docs and type it from scratch
B) I open Claude and enter brief notes
C) I give Claude the approved email, role, context and task, then review the draft
D) I use a reviewed skill such as `/customer-reply`

**Scenario 2, Delegation:** You need a job advertisement.
A) I open Word and type it from scratch
B) I ask Claude to "write a job advertisement"
C) I provide the role, approved company context, work profile and salary range
D) I use a maintained Project brief and specify only the case-specific details

**Scenario 3, Automation:** A website form inquiry arrives.
A) I copy it into the CRM manually
B) The form writes to the CRM
C) The form writes to the CRM and prepares a reply draft for review
D) An approved workflow handles routing, drafting and review assignment

**Scenario 4, Knowledge:** A manager asks what was decided about a subject in January.
A) I rely on memory
B) I search email, Notion and file storage
C) I query an approved knowledge tool and open the cited record
D) I use a maintained decision-log workflow with source links

**Scenario 5, Governance:** A colleague asks whether customer data may be entered into ChatGPT.
A) I do not know
B) I assume GDPR prohibits it
C) I classify the data and apply the approved tool policy
D) I refer to a maintained AI policy and escalation owner

_(Scenarios 6 to 10 are in the Fluency Test on the AI-Native page.)_
sections.keyTakeaway: Same scoring rule on every run. The result is a starting value, not a qualification.

sections.title: What your score tells you
sections.content:
**How this course reads the result:**
- **0 to 2 per dimension:** little observed use; pick one controlled practice task
- **3 to 4 per dimension:** regular, but not yet across every suitable task
- **5 to 6 per dimension:** consistent use of the assessed behaviors

There is no comparison value here. This course has not measured a representative average, and you do not measure yourself against an unsupported number.

You are your own benchmark. Repeat the test after Modules 2 to 4 and compare the evidence behind each answer: completed workflows, source checks, approvals, governance controls.
sections.keyTakeaway: Your own score, measured again and evidenced. This course claims no population comparison.

quiz.questionText: What are the five dimensions in this AI-Native Fluency assessment?

answerOptions.text: Typing, reading, calculating, analyzing and presenting
Drafting, delegation, automation, knowledge and governance
Input, output, quality, speed and cost
Tools, skills, workflows, data and results

quiz.explanation: The five dimensions are drafting, delegation, automation, knowledge and governance.

quiz.questionText: Which baseline should you use to measure progress?

answerOptions.text: An unsupported industry average
Your own score using the same scenarios and criteria
The highest score reported by another learner
A score generated by Claude without evidence

quiz.explanation: Record your own baseline and repeat the same assessment. This course does not claim a representative average.
